text:
Selection outside the loop

1from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, f_classif
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, StratifiedKFold

2keep = SelectKBest(f_classif, k=20).fit(X, y).get_support()
3X_kept = X[:, keep]

4cv = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=363)
5leaky = cross_val_score(KNeighborsClassifier(5), X_kept, y, cv=cv)
float(leaky.mean().round(3))


1

SelectKBest ranks predictors by a scoring function and keeps the top
k; f_classif is the ANOVA F-statistic between each column of X and the class label y.

2

SelectKBest(f_classif, k=20).fit(X, y) scores all 2000 columns against
the full y and keeps the top 20; .get_support() returns a boolean mask of which columns were kept, assigned to keep. Fitting on the full X and y before any split is the leak.

3

X[:, keep] uses that boolean mask to select only the 20 chosen
columns, assigned to X_kept.

4

StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=363) builds 5 folds that
preserve the class proportions of y in each fold.

5

cross_val_score(KNeighborsClassifier(5), X_kept, y, cv=cv)
cross-validates a 5-nearest-neighbors classifier on X_kept, the already-selected columns, so every fold’s “test” data already influenced which columns were chosen.




0.85




We cross-validated. Why is this not 0.5?

Pipeline takes a list of (name, step) pairs. SelectKBest(f_classif,      k=20) is now the "select" step inside the pipeline, so scikit-learn refits it on each training fold alone rather than on the full data.

2

object, so SelectKBest and KNeighborsClassifier(5) are both refit from scratch on each fold’s training rows, exactly like leaky above but with the selection step properly inside the loop.

Missing data

Imputation is estimation. An imputed value is a prediction, and it must be learned on the training fold.



Dropping rows discards information and biases the result

Filling with a column mean is a model, and a weak one

For prediction, missingness itself is often informative

title: Pipelines and data leakage
text:
SimpleImputer

from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsRegressor

num_steps = Pipeline([
1    ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
2    ("scale", StandardScaler()),
])

prep = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", num_steps, num),
3    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", handle_unknown="ignore"), cat),
])

4full = Pipeline([("prep", prep), ("knn", KNeighborsRegressor(5))])


1

SimpleImputer(strategy="median") replaces missing values in a numeric
column with that column’s median, computed only from the training fold it is fit on.

2

("scale", StandardScaler()) runs second, so scaling happens after
imputation fills the gaps, still learned from the training fold alone.

3

OneHotEncoder(drop="first", handle_unknown="ignore") adds
handle_unknown="ignore" so a category value seen in a test fold but never seen while fitting on the training fold produces all zero indicator columns instead of raising an error.

4

full chains the entire prep (imputation, scaling, and encoding) with
KNeighborsRegressor(5) into a single estimator, so calling .fit on full fits every preprocessing step and the model together.

title: Pipelines and data leakage
text:
Repeated measures

Repeated measurements on the same subject are correlated with each other, not independent draws. A random split can put one subject’s rows in both the training fold and the test fold.



A nearest-neighbor model can then “recognize” the subject, since its near-duplicate points sit right there in the training data, instead of generalizing to a subject it has never seen.

title: Pipelines and data leakage
text:
GroupKFold

GroupKFold folds on the group label, not the row: every row from a given subject lands entirely in the training set or entirely in the test set, never split between them.



Pass it a groups array, one label per row, patient_id here. The fold assignment respects that label instead of splitting row by row.

Look-ahead leakage

A predictor recorded after the outcome can look powerful in cross-validation and be useless at prediction time, since it is a consequence of the outcome rather than something known when the prediction is needed.



The question is not “is this correlated with the outcome.” It is “would I have this value at the moment I need to make the prediction.”

1from sklearn.preprocessing import SplineTransformer
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error

2dfs = range(4, 51, 4)
train_mse, test_mse = [], []

for df in dfs:
3    model = make_pipeline(SplineTransformer(degree=3, n_knots=df - 2), LinearRegression())
4    model.fit(x_train.reshape(-1, 1), y_train)
5    train_mse.append(mean_squared_error(y_train, model.predict(x_train.reshape(-1, 1))))
    test_mse.append(mean_squared_error(y_test, model.predict(x_test.reshape(-1, 1))))


1

SplineTransformer builds a B-spline basis expansion of a predictor,
the tool used here for a flexible, well-conditioned curve.

2

dfs = range(4, 51, 4) is the sequence of degrees of freedom to sweep:
4, 8, 12, …, 48, from rigid to wiggly.

3

make_pipeline chains two steps. SplineTransformer(degree=3,      n_knots=df - 2) builds a cubic (degree=3) spline basis with df - 2 interior knots, giving the basis df total degrees of freedom. LinearRegression() then fits ordinary least squares on that basis.

4

model.fit(x_train.reshape(-1, 1), y_train) fits the pipeline on the
training data only; .reshape(-1, 1) turns the 1-D array x_train into the 2-D shape scikit-learn expects.

5

mean_squared_error(y_train, model.predict(...)) computes the training
MSE at this df and appends it to train_mse; the same pattern on the next line (not separately annotated) computes the test MSE into test_mse.

Variance, defined

How much \(\hat{f}\) would change if estimated from a different training set. Different training data gives a different \(\hat{f}\); a good method should not move too much between them.

Why flexible methods have high variance

A flexible fit follows the training points closely, so changing even a few of those points can change the fit a lot.



An inflexible line barely moves when one point changes. Why?

text:
Bias, defined

The error from approximating a complicated relationship with a simpler model. A method that cannot bend enough to match \(f\) is biased, no matter how much data it sees.

title: Bias-variance trade-off

The bias formula
\[\text{Bias}(\hat{f}(x_0)) = E[\hat{f}(x_0)] - {\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$f(x_0)$}}\]

\[\text{CV}_{(n)} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\text{MSE}_i\]

title: Cross-validation
text:
LOOCV
\[\text{CV}_{(n)} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$\text{MSE}_i$}}\]
The MSE from the single fold where observation \(i\) was held out and every other observation trained the model.

title: Cross-validation
text:
LOOCV
\[\text{CV}_{(n)} = \frac{1}{n}{\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$\sum_{i=1}^{n}$}}\text{MSE}_i\]
Add that leave-one-out MSE up over all \(n\) observations, since each gets a turn.

title: Cross-validation
text:
LOOCV
\[\text{CV}_{(n)} = {\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$\frac{1}{n}$}}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\text{MSE}_i\]
Divide by \(n\) to average it, exactly like training or test MSE.

title: Cross-validation
text:
LOOCV looks expensive

With \(n\) observations we fit \(n\) models. For regression fit using least squares, there is a shortcut avoids refitting entirely.

title: Cross-validation
text:
The LOOCV shortcut
\[\text{CV}_{(n)} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\frac{y_i - \hat{y}_i}{1 - h_i}\right)^2\]

title: Cross-validation
text:
The LOOCV shortcut
\[\text{CV}_{(n)} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\frac{y_i - {\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$\hat{y}_i$}}}{1 - h_i}\right)^2\]
The fitted value from the single model fit on all \(n\) observations. No refitting.

title: Cross-validation
text:
The LOOCV shortcut
\[\text{CV}_{(n)} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\frac{y_i - \hat{y}_i}{1 - {\require{color}\colorbox{#eec8e1}{$h_i$}}}\right)^2\]
The leverage of observation \(i\): how much that point influences its own fit. Dividing by \(1 - h_i\) inflates high-leverage residuals by exactly enough to match what leaving that point out would have given.

We’ll come back to this to define \(h_i\) in the linear regression section

title: Cross-validation
text:
Choosing k: bias

LOOCV trains on \(n - 1\) points: almost the whole data set, so almost no bias

\(k\)-fold trains on about \((k-1)n/k\) points: fewer, so a little more bias

The validation set approach trains on about half: the most bias of the three




By bias alone, LOOCV wins.

title: Cross-validation
text:
Choosing k: variance

LOOCV’s \(n\) fits are trained on nearly identical data, so their errors are highly correlated. Averaging correlated quantities does not shrink variance the way averaging independent ones does.



\(k\)-fold’s fits overlap less, so their errors correlate less, and the average is more stable. In practice \(k = 5\) or \(k = 10\) balances both.
